name: Communism
info: Communism seeks a classless society of common ownership, without private property, money or the state; first named in 18th-century France and redefined by Marx and Engels in 1848, it guided the Soviet Union, China and other one-party states.

facts.thinkers: François-Noël Babeuf, Nicolas Restif de la Bretonne and Sylvain Maréchal, in James H. Billington’s view the progenitors of modern communism; Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels, founders of Marxism; Vladimir Lenin, theorist of the vanguard party; Joseph Stalin, who developed Marxism–Leninism; Leon Trotsky, of permanent revolution; Mao Zedong; Peter Kropotkin, main theorist of anarcho-communism
facts.texts: Thomas More’s Utopia (1516), an early picture of common ownership; The Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels (1848); Friedrich Engels’s The Peasant War in Germany (1850); Eduard Bernstein’s Cromwell and Communism (1895); Marx’s Grundrisse and The Civil War in France, on which libertarian Marxists draw
facts.ideas: common ownership of the means of production, distribution and exchange; class struggle between the proletariat and the bourgeoisie; historical materialism; the dictatorship of the proletariat as the transition; distribution “from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs”; the end of social classes, money and the state
facts.today: as of 2026 China, Cuba, Laos, North Korea and Vietnam are ruled by Communist parties under single-party systems, all but North Korea allowing more economic competition; Communist parties have shared power democratically in Nepal and sit in governing coalitions in Brazil and Uruguay; the Progressive Party of the Working People won 22.3% of the vote in Cyprus in 2026; remnants of Peru’s Shining Path are still active

t: Marx and Engels gave communism its modern definition in The Communist Manifesto of 1848: a classless society, reached through proletarian revolution, in which goods would be shared according to need.

From the Russian Revolution of 1917 Communist governments spread to Eastern Europe, Asia and other regions, and for much of the 20th century more than one-third of the world’s population lived under them.

Communist states were marked by one-party rule, state control of the economy and the media, and the suppression of opposition; estimates of the deaths under them range from 10–20 million to over 100 million and remain disputed.
dyk: One of the first uses of the word in its modern sense is in a letter of around 1785 in which Victor d’Hupay called himself an auteur communiste, a “communist author”.
ev: Nicolas Restif de la Bretonne uses communisme for a social order based on equality and the common ownership of property
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish The Communist Manifesto, offering a new definition of communism
The October Revolution brings Lenin’s Bolsheviks to power in Russia, the first avowedly communist party to take state power
The Bolsheviks found the Comintern, dedicated to promoting revolution throughout the world
Stalin’s Great Purge begins; in the Moscow trials leading old Bolsheviks are accused, plead guilty to conspiracy and are executed
Mao Zedong and the Chinese Communist Party come to power in China at the end of the Chinese Civil War
Mao’s Cultural Revolution begins, a ten-year upheaval that targets intellectuals and party leaders
The Soviet Union is dissolved, after the Revolutions of 1989 have brought down most of the Eastern Bloc

sections.origins:
The word comes from the Latin communis, common. According to Richard Pipes the idea of a classless, egalitarian society first emerged in ancient Greece, and Plato has been considered the first author to give communism serious thought. The 5th-century Mazdak movement in Persia, which challenged the privileges of nobles and clergy and the institution of private property, has been called communistic, as have the Waldensians and the Hutterites. Thomas Müntzer led a large Anabaptist communist movement in the German Peasants’ War, Thomas More portrayed a society of common property in Utopia (1516), and in 17th-century England the Diggers called for an end to private ownership of land.

Criticism of private property continued in the Enlightenment with Mably, Meslier, Morelly and Rousseau. Victor d’Hupay called himself a communist author around 1785, and in 1793 Restif de la Bretonne used communisme for a social order of equality and common property. In James H. Billington’s view Babeuf, Restif and Sylvain Maréchal, all active in the French Revolution, were the progenitors of modern communism.

In the early 19th century Robert Owen founded New Harmony, Indiana, in 1825, and Fourier’s followers founded Brook Farm in 1841. As the Industrial Revolution advanced, socialist critics blamed capitalism for the misery of the proletariat of factory workers, and in 1848 Marx and Engels offered a new definition of communism in The Communist Manifesto.
sections.ideas:
Communists hold that the present order stems from capitalism, which divides society into two classes: the proletariat, the majority, who must sell their labour power to survive, and the bourgeoisie, a minority that profits from owning the means of production. The relationship is exploitative and, in their view, can be resolved only by social revolution, which would put the working class in power and establish common ownership. Marxism grounds this in historical materialism, which holds that history is shaped by modes of production and that the change from one to the next is driven by class struggle.

Between capitalism and communism stands the dictatorship of the proletariat, based on the model of the Paris Commune and meant to be the most democratic of states, with all public authority elected and recallable. A socialist stage, “to each according to his contribution”, would give way, as productive forces advanced, to a classless, stateless society run on the maxim “from each according to his ability, to each according to his needs”. Marxism sets socialisation, control of property by society, above nationalisation, which in Engels’s words does not do away with the capitalist nature of the productive forces.

Communists disagree on the means. Leninists rely on a vanguard party of professional revolutionaries bound by democratic centralism; libertarian communists favour workers’ councils and self-management; anarcho-communists such as Peter Kropotkin wanted society to pass at once to communism, without a state.
sections.spread:
The word fell out of use by the 1860s, and by 1888 Marxists used socialism instead. After the October Revolution of 1917 Lenin made socialism a stage between capitalism and communism, and in 1918 the Bolsheviks renamed their party the Communist Party. The Comintern, founded in 1919, carried the Bolshevik model abroad, while council communism, which arose in Germany and the Netherlands in the 1920s, and left communism opposed it.

After Lenin’s death Marxism–Leninism, resting on dialectical materialism, the leading role of the party and a planned economy with industrialisation and collectivisation, became the official ideology of Communist parties; at its height it covered at least a third of the world’s population. Trotskyism, which upheld permanent and world revolution against Stalin’s socialism in one country, founded the Fourth International in 1938. China and the Soviet Union were at sword’s point by 1960, splitting the world movement into two hostile camps, and anti-revisionists such as the Maoists and Enver Hoxha’s followers rejected the Soviet line after Khrushchev.

Governments modelled on the Soviet Union took power with Soviet help in Bulgaria, Czechoslovakia, East Germany, Poland, Hungary and Romania after the Second World War; Tito’s Yugoslavia broke with Stalin in 1948, and the Cuban revolutionaries who overthrew Batista in 1959 became Marxist–Leninist. In Western Europe communist parties joined post-war governments and in the 1970s developed Eurocommunism, and since 1957 communists have often won power in the Indian state of Kerala.
sections.power:
The Bolsheviks gave the land of the church and nobility to the peasants but took their surplus grain, shut down opposing newspapers and founded the Cheka as a secret police; in January 1918 they dissolved the Constituent Assembly, in which they had won 23.3% of the vote to the Socialist Revolutionaries’ 37.6%. War communism forbade strikes and imposed labour duty, and in March 1921 the Red Army crushed a workers’ uprising at Kronstadt. In the Great Purge of 1936–1938 Stalin set out to destroy any possible opposition in the party, and old Bolsheviks such as Kamenev, Zinoviev, Rykov and Bukharin were tried and executed; the secret police went on sending suspects to the gulag. The state also built a vast research effort, and the Soviet Union launched the world’s first space satellite.

In China the Great Leap Forward of 1957–1961 put peasants into large collective farms ordered to start heavy industry; agricultural output fell sharply, causing mass famine and millions of deaths. In the Cultural Revolution of 1966–1976 millions were accused, humiliated and imprisoned, killed or sent to work as farm labourers. Estimates of the victims of Mao’s government range from 40 to 80 million, through starvation, persecution, prison labour and mass executions; Mao is also praised for advances in literacy, women’s rights, healthcare and life expectancy.

Estimates of all deaths under Communist states range from 10–20 million to over 100 million; scholars dispute the higher figures and whether the killings were genocide.
sections.critiques:
Criticism of communism falls into two kinds: of the practice of 20th-century Communist states, and of Marxist principles and theory. Ludwig von Mises argued that by abolishing free markets, communist officials would lack the price system needed to guide planned production. Planned enterprises hoarded labour and inputs amid chronic shortages and, in the theory of János Kornai, worked under a soft budget constraint; by 1988 output per person in the former planned economies of Central and Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union was about 43 percent of that in the OECD countries. The decline of communism has been attributed to economic inefficiency and to authoritarianism and bureaucracy within its governments.

Many communists criticised the Soviet path too. Mensheviks and social democrats thought Russia too backward for a socialist revolution; council and left communists held that the Bolsheviks had built state capitalism, and Trotsky called the Soviet Union under Stalin a degenerated workers’ state.

The death toll is debated. John Gray, Daniel Goldhagen and Richard Pipes see communist ideology as a significant cause of mass killings, while genocide scholars do not consider ideology or regime type an important factor and hold that most Communist states did not carry out mass killings. Mark Bradley wrote that the exact numbers are disputed but the order of magnitude is not. According to Dovid Katz and other historians, a double genocide view equating these deaths with the Holocaust is popular in Eastern Europe; some Western scholars reject the comparison.
sections.legacy:
Public memory of the Communist states has been described as a battleground between anti-communism and anti-anti-communism. The Black Book of Communism, whose figure of 100 million victims is the estimate the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation most commonly uses, though some of its own authors distanced themselves from it, helped legitimise comparisons of Nazism and Stalinism, and museums and monuments to the victims stand in Eastern Europe, Canada and the United States. The sociologist András Bozóki set social mobility, the elimination of illiteracy, more accessible healthcare and housing and free higher education against the suppression of freedom, a culture of fear and corruption and closed societies.

After 1989 and 1991 mortality rose sharply in the former Soviet countries, while the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia saw life expectancy rise. By 2019 most Eastern Europeans approved of multiparty democracy and a market economy, and 61 percent said living standards were higher than under Communism. Gary Gerstle and Walter Scheidel argue that fear of communism made Western elites readier to compromise with labour, and that the welfare state declined as the threat waned.

China’s reform and opening up from 1978 brought the poverty rate down from 53% in the Mao era to 8% in 2001, and Vietnam and Cuba have turned toward the market, while North Korea keeps Soviet-style communism.

summary: Communism is the ideology of a classless, stateless society based on common ownership. Given its modern definition by Marx and Engels in 1848, it took power in Russia in 1917 and later ruled more than a third of the world’s population; its one-party states industrialised and spread literacy, but also carried out purges, famines and repression whose death toll is still debated.
references: Richard Pipes, Communism: A History (Modern Library, 2003)
Robert Service, Comrades!: A History of World Communism (Harvard University Press, 2010)
David Priestland, The Red Flag: A History of Communism (Grove Press, 2009)
François Furet, The Passing of an Illusion: The Idea of Communism in the Twentieth Century (University of Chicago Press, 2000)
Silvio Pons and Robert Service, eds., A Dictionary of 20th Century Communism (Princeton University Press, 2010)
Grigore Pop-Eleches and Joshua A. Tucker, Communism’s Shadow: Historical Legacies and Contemporary Political Attitudes (Princeton University Press, 2017)
notes: Start 1793: Restif's first use of communisme for a social order of common property; the article also gives d'Hupay's 'communist author' around 1785 (dyk), places communism's emergence as a political doctrine in the French Revolution (Babeuf, Restif, Maréchal), and gives 1848 as the Manifesto's new definition. 1848 would be the alternative if the editor wants the Marxist definition.

The Great Leap Forward is dated '1957–1961' in this article (the Maoism article dates its famine 1958–1961 and the Anti-Rightist Campaign 1957–1958); I kept this article's dates here. The article says Mao 'and his top aide Deng Xiaoping launched' it; I left Deng out of the sentence to keep it short.

Death tolls given only as the article attributes them: Mao's government 40 to 80 million (no author named in the article); all Communist states 10–20 million to over 100 million, with the criticism of the higher estimates; 100 million from The Black Book of Communism. No figure is given for the Great Purge, the gulag or Soviet famines; the article names only the 1946–1947 famine, 'the worst natural famine in over fifty years', which I left out. Holodomor and the Khmer Rouge's killings are not described in the article (Pol Pot is named only in the scholars' comparison), so they are absent.
The 1988 GDP comparison is for 'the CEE/CIS area' against the OECD on IMF estimates; I wrote 'the former planned economies of Central and Eastern Europe and the Soviet Union'.
The article lists the remaining Communist states 'as of 2026'. The Nepal power-sharing is described in the past and present; I wrote 'have shared power democratically'.

Left out: the 1917 election details beyond the two figures, Christian communism, Eurocommunism's leaders, the CMEA's problems, Lysenkoism (it says Lysenkoism 'is widely believed to have contributed to the Great Chinese Famine').
